title: After the Land Acknowledgment, Keep Following the Story
subtitle: A venue’s statement can be a starting point. Here’s how to learn about the Nation it names, look for Indigenous-led sources and ask what the institution does beyond its words.
imageAlt: Two friends sit together in a museum gallery, one reading a land acknowledgment on a phone while the other looks at a nearby exhibit label.
imageConcept: Two friends in a quiet cultural venue, seated near a gallery entrance with a phone open to the venue’s land acknowledgment and the exhibit visible beyond them.
body: A statement is a beginning, not a visit

You might encounter a land acknowledgment on a museum wall, a library website, a theater program or a welcome before an event. It names Indigenous peoples and their relationship to the place where the institution operates. That can be meaningful—but reading the statement is not the same as learning the story, and the statement alone cannot tell you what the institution does in the present.

A useful way to continue is to visit with someone you trust and treat the acknowledgment as a prompt for inquiry, not a scorecard. Read what the venue says, note the Nation or Nations it names, then look for public information from those Nations or Indigenous-led organizations. Afterward, return to the venue’s own materials and see whether they point to ongoing relationships, commitments or action. The aim is not to produce a verdict from one webpage. It is to leave with a clearer sense of what you learned and one good place to keep learning.
Keep Indigenous people in the present tense

A common limitation of public acknowledgments is that they can describe Indigenous presence as something that belongs chiefly to the past. Reporting by April Rubin in Axios includes Indigenous experts’ concerns about statements that are not paired with ongoing action and that leave Indigenous people out of the present [1]. That concern matters in a cultural venue, where an institution’s language can shape how visitors understand whose stories are alive now.

As you read, notice the verbs and time markers. Does the wording name Indigenous people as part of the community today, or speak only of who lived here before? Does it mention continuing relationships or responsibilities, or stop after naming a history? These are observations, not a checklist that settles whether an acknowledgment is adequate. A short statement may have limits; a longer one may still be disconnected from meaningful work. Let the wording raise questions rather than answer them for you.
Treat the Nation’s name as a search beginning

Write down the name exactly as the venue presents it. Then use that as a first search term, not as proof that you have the full picture. Look for a Nation’s own government website or an Indigenous-led organization’s public information. Seek current material: a cultural program, a community priority, a public event, a news update or an explanation of the Nation’s work. If the venue names more than one Nation, keep each name in view rather than collapsing them into one story.

This step helps correct a basic misunderstanding: tribal Nations are not simply cultural references or chapters of local history. The National Congress of American Indians’ introduction describes tribal Nations as contemporary political entities [2]. That distinction matters when a venue’s wording makes a Nation sound like an emblem of the past. It also gives you a practical reason to prioritize the Nation’s own public sources: they can speak to present-day governance and priorities in ways a venue’s brief acknowledgment may not.
Make a small, careful research pass

You do not need to become an expert to make the next step useful. Set a modest limit—perhaps twenty minutes—and divide the time. First, read the venue’s statement and note the Nation’s name, the date you accessed it and any linked material. Next, search the Nation’s official public channels. If a search result is ambiguous, check whether the page is maintained by the Nation or an Indigenous-led organization before relying on it. Save one current source that you would be comfortable returning to.

As you read, ask: What does this source say is happening now? What does it identify as important? Is there a public event, cultural offering or community resource that you can learn about directly? Avoid treating one source as a complete account of a Nation’s history or views. Nations differ, and no single page can stand in for all members or all local contexts. The point is to follow the lead of public, Indigenous-led information rather than ask an Indigenous visitor or staff member to supply a personal lesson.
Look back at what the venue makes visible

Now return to the museum, library, theater or other venue’s public materials. Search its site for the acknowledgment and for related pages about Indigenous partnerships, programming, collections, hiring, funding or community relationships. These categories are prompts for looking, not assumptions that every venue should use the same model. Notice what the institution actually says, whether the information is current and whether it identifies a relationship or action beyond the statement.

Keep the distinction between what you find and what you infer. “The page names a partnership” is an observation; “the institution has repaired its relationship” is a much larger conclusion. If the venue’s materials do not explain what happens beyond the acknowledgment, you can record that gap without deciding from a single page what the institution does or does not do elsewhere. A careful reader can hold both things at once: the statement may matter, and the public information may not yet show the larger picture.
Action has more than one shape

There is no universal template for what a cultural institution’s next steps should be. The Native Governance Center’s guide encourages attention to Indigenous past, present and future, and to concrete action beyond acknowledgment [3]. The guide suggests possible actions such as recurring donations to Native-led organizations and voluntary land-tax programs [3]. Those examples are not a menu for every venue to copy; they show that action can take forms more substantial than adding another sentence to a statement.

For your visit, use the examples as a reminder to ask what the institution itself describes—not to prescribe a specific action on behalf of a Nation. A venue may point visitors toward an ongoing relationship, a community-directed initiative or a public program. If it does, follow the details and who is leading the work. If it does not, that absence tells you what the public materials made visible, not everything that may be happening behind the scenes.
Talk with your companion without turning it into a test

If you visit with a friend, compare notes after you have each looked at the materials. What did you learn from the Nation’s own public source that the venue’s statement did not explain? What did the venue make easy to find, and what required more searching? Did either of you notice language that placed Indigenous people in the past rather than the present? These questions keep the conversation specific and leave room for different readings.

Try not to turn the discussion into a contest over who found the most information or a demand that one person resolve every uncertainty. Neither friend needs to speak for a Nation. If the topic brings up a question that cannot be answered from reliable public material, it is reasonable to leave it open. Curiosity is not a license to expect unpaid explanation from Indigenous people you meet at the venue. A more respectful next step is often simply to keep reading sources that the Nation or Indigenous-led organizations have chosen to make public.
Leave with one source and one open question

Before you move on, save one reliable source from the Nation or an Indigenous-led organization, along with the venue’s acknowledgment page. Add a short note about what each page helped you understand and what remains unclear. If you want to continue, check the Nation’s public channels for a program or update, or revisit the venue’s materials later to see whether they have added information about an ongoing relationship. You are not obliged to turn a single visit into a campaign or an institutional evaluation.

The exercise is small by design: read, follow the name, compare public information and keep one useful source. It shifts attention away from polishing acknowledgment language and toward the living people and institutions connected to the place. The venue may be a gateway into that learning, but it is not the final authority on the Nation’s story. Let the visit end with something more durable than a feeling of completion: a source you can return to, and an understanding that learning continues.
